This report outlines that there's currently two capital reserves that help to support our waste collections and diversion programs for the city's various waste programs.
This report is recommending to combine the two reserves to improve flexibility in delivering programs and create a more sustainable funding framework.

More specifically, this report outlines proposed changes to the waste container replacement reserve in response to significant shifts in how waste collection programs in Saskatoon are funded and delivered.
The residential waste and organics services have transition to utility funded models.
Additional multi waste programs are currently being planned.
And responsibility for residential recycling is expected to transfer to Saskter cycles in 2028.
Together these changes reduce or eliminate key revenue sources that historically have supported capital investments for waste services,
including funding that flowed through the waste minimization reserve.
As a result, the current structure of the reserve framework no longer aligns with future service and funding requirements.
To address this, the report recommends specifically renaming the waste container replacement reserve to the waste utility capital reserve.

And expanding its purpose to fund all waste collection related capital needs, including vehicles, facilities, service efficiency improvements and as well as various initiatives under the solid waste reduction and diversion plan.
Also recommends transferring the remaining funds from the waste minimization reserve, totaling 5.1 million into the new reserve and closing that waste minimization reserve.
These changes, as mentioned, will consolidate capital funding for waste utilities into a single reserve.
It will support long-term financial sustainability and provide the flexibility required to meet growth, service and environmental objectives with no disruption to approved waste utility operations.

This report provides an overview of the city of Saskatoon's indigenous apprenticeship program in fleet services and other indigenous focused work placements in the city.
In October 2025, the administration signed a partnership agreement with Saskto and Travel Council for the initiation of an indigenous apprenticeship program.

The program provides training opportunities for apprentices to complete a four year heavy duty equipment apprenticeship program and achieve a red seal journey person certificate while working in fleet services.
The program was officially launched in March, 2021 with a recruitment of two indigenous apprentices and is jointly funded by the city and STC.

The heavy duty mechanics and fleet services are members of QP859 local union. The union has been a strong support of the partnership between the city and STC and has signed a memorandum agreement with the city in support of the program and its framework.
This agreement facilitated the implementation of the program in the city's unionized work environment.
The labour market for a journey person mechanics has been very competitive in recent years. In 2024 and 2025, fleet services could not feel several vacant positions for over a year.
Once the apprentices complete the program and achieve their red seal journey person certificates, they will be able to apply for vacant journey person mechanic positions in fleet services.
The indigenous apprenticeship program is taking a reconciliation approach through partnership between the city and STC.

Grounded in ceremony, cultural safety and shared decision making, the program aims to remove systemic barriers, create meaningful employment pathways for indigenous peoples and build a culturally safe municipal workplace.
This program demonstrates reconciliation and action by moving beyond intent to sustain measurable practice.
The success of the program will be defined by the sustained cultural and organizational conditions that enable indigenous apprentices to thrive.

Programs success assessment will include qualitative indicators such as skills development, readiness for next steps, improved recruitment reach, supervisor readiness, cultural responsive practices, sustained partnership with the indigenous organizations and community trust.

The assessment will also include quantifiable indicators such as the apprentice's time on tools, completion of the annual year end exams, safety performance in the busy shop environment, completion of the apprenticeship program and then seal red seal exam.
Apprentice detention rate upon their completion of the program and other factors such as attendance, quality of work accountability and alignment with corporate values and core of conduct.
